Chapter 3: The International Tribunal and the Politics of Justice
Imagine, for a moment, the creation of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. It really was a bold experiment—an effort to prove to the world that mass murder wouldn’t go unpunished, and that no matter how powerful, those responsible for terrible crimes would be held to account.
But as the tribunal’s work in Kosovo got underway, the truth became clear: the road to justice was anything but simple.
Inside the tribunal, you’d find this fascinating blend of idealism and hard-nosed realism. Many of the people there were driven by a deep sense of purpose. They truly believed the law could make a difference—that it could offer at least some justice to those who had suffered so much.
At the same time, everyone understood there were limits. The tribunal itself was the result of tough international compromise, shaped by powerful countries and the political realities left behind after the war.
Just bringing a single case to trial was slow and exhausting. Prosecutors had to put together mountains of evidence, often collected under nearly impossible conditions. Witnesses needed protection, their identities carefully hidden from anyone who might want to silence them. Every decision was picked apart—by governments, the press, and the global public.
Political pressure was never far away. Some countries, hoping to keep the Balkans stable, pushed for more lenient treatment or even delays. Others, still haunted by their own failure to stop the violence, demanded the tribunal take action fast. So the tribunal was always walking a tightrope—trying to balance justice with the fear of making things worse.
And then there was the heavy shadow of denial. Many people in the region simply refused to believe that crimes had been committed in their name. Some saw the tribunal as foreign meddling, believing it only punished one side and ignored the suffering of others. The team of investigators and prosecutors had to deal not just with legal challenges, but with a deep resistance to the very idea of being held accountable.
Inside the courtroom, the tension was real. The accused weren’t just ordinary people; they were often powerful men—former army commanders or politicians. Their trials were watched closely, not just in the Balkans, but around the world. For survivors, being there was a chance to tell their story, to finally have their pain recognized. For the accused, it was a test of whether the international community truly meant what it said about justice.
The process was far from perfect. Delays happened all the time, and the results weren't always satisfying. Some defendants walked free, while others got sentences that many thought were just too light. The tribunal faced criticism from all sides—sometimes for going too far, and sometimes for not going far enough.
And yet, even with all its flaws, the tribunal marked a real step forward. It showed that the world was willing to face the ugly truth of mass atrocity, even when it was uncomfortable or messy. It gave at least some measure of justice to families who had lost everything. And maybe most importantly, it sent a message: once the truth is uncovered, it can’t just be buried again.
For those who worked at the tribunal, the experience was life-changing. Many started out full of hope, only to run headlong into the complicated, often messy reality of international justice. They discovered that accountability isn’t just about the law. It’s about politics, memory, and having the courage to face difficult truths.
In the end, the tribunal’s real legacy wasn’t just its verdicts. It was its insistence that the world can’t, and shouldn’t, turn away from the horrors of war.
